title: Introduction to Network Flow
description: Push as much flow as possible from a source to a sink through capacitated edges

sections.title: 11. The Max Flow Min Cut Connection
12. Pitfalls and How to Approach It

blocks.text: Network flow models the movement of something, water, data, goods, through a network of pipes that each have a limited capacity. The central question is how much can flow from a starting point to a destination at once.
This one framework solves a surprising range of problems, from matching and scheduling to connectivity, because so many questions can be rephrased as pushing flow through a network.

blocks.caption: A flow network: edges carry flow up to their capacity from source to sink
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406761806-501143383.png

By the end of this topic you will understand what a flow network is, the rules flow must obey, the maximum flow problem, and the augmenting path method that solves it, including the crucial idea of a residual graph. It is one of the most powerful tools in graph theory.
The reason network flow feels magical is that so many problems in disguise are really flow problems. Learning to spot that disguise is half the value of this topic.
Keep the pipes and water image in your head throughout; every formal rule maps neatly onto it.

A flow network is a directed graph where each edge has a capacity, the maximum amount that can flow along it. Two special nodes are singled out: a source where flow originates and a sink where it is collected.
You can picture it as a system of pipes. Each pipe has a width limiting how much water it carries, and you want to send as much water as possible from the source tap to the sink drain.

items: A directed graph with a capacity on every edge
A source node where flow starts
A sink node where flow ends
Capacities limit how much can travel along each edge

blocks.text:
The pipe analogy:

Think of edges as pipes and capacity as pipe width. Flow is the water, and the goal is to move as much as possible from source to sink without bursting any pipe.
In the example network, the source can send up to 10 units toward A and 5 toward B, and both eventually funnel into the sink through their own capacities.

items: Directed edges, each with a capacity
One source that produces flow
One sink that absorbs flow
Everything in between merely routes flow along

blocks.text: A valid flow assigns an amount to each edge, subject to two rules. First, the flow on any edge cannot exceed its capacity. Second, flow is conserved.

blocks.caption: At every node except source and sink, flow in must equal flow out
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406761806-80057789.png

Conservation means that at every node except the source and sink, the total flow coming in equals the total flow going out. Nothing is created or lost in the middle, just like water through a junction of pipes.

items: Capacity rule: flow on an edge is at most its capacity
Conservation rule: at inner nodes, flow in equals flow out
The source produces flow and the sink absorbs it
The value of a flow is the total leaving the source

blocks.text: Conservation is what keeps a flow physically sensible. If more entered a junction than left it, water would be piling up, which is not allowed.
The value of the whole flow is measured at the source: it is the net amount leaving the source toward the rest of the network.
The central task is the maximum flow problem: given the network, find the largest possible value of flow from source to sink that still obeys the capacity and conservation rules.

Intuitively, you are limited by bottlenecks. A narrow pipe somewhere along the way caps how much can get through, no matter how wide the other pipes are. Max flow finds the best way to route around and through those bottlenecks.

items: Maximise the total flow from source to sink
Respect every edge capacity
Keep flow conserved at all inner nodes
Bottleneck edges limit the achievable total

blocks.text: The word bottleneck is literal here. Somewhere along the way the narrowest crossing caps the total, and max flow is about using every route to get past those narrow points.

Bottlenecks rule the total:

No matter how wide the other pipes are, the tightest crossing between source and sink limits how much can get through.
Solving it well means routing flow across many paths at once, splitting and combining streams to squeeze the most through the network.
The classic way to build up the maximum flow is through augmenting paths. An augmenting path is a route from source to sink where every edge still has some spare capacity.

blocks.caption: Find a source to sink path with spare capacity and push flow along it
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406761806-369093035.png

If such a path exists, you can push more flow along it, limited by the smallest spare capacity on the path, called the bottleneck. You repeat this, finding path after path and adding flow, until no augmenting path remains.

The bottleneck rule:

On any augmenting path you can only push as much as its tightest edge allows. That smallest spare capacity is the amount of new flow the path contributes.
Each augmenting path adds a little more to the total, and the algorithm simply keeps finding them until the network is saturated.
The amount you add is never more than the tightest edge on the chosen path allows.
The key idea that makes augmenting paths correct is the residual graph. It tracks, for every edge, how much more flow could still be pushed, and importantly, how much could be pushed back.

blocks.caption: The residual graph tracks spare forward capacity and cancellable backward flow
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406761807-437468904.png

Each original edge contributes two residual capacities: a forward one equal to capacity minus current flow, and a backward one equal to the flow already sent. The backward capacity lets a later path cancel earlier flow, which is what lets the algorithm correct mistakes.

items: Forward residual: remaining capacity, capacity minus flow
Backward residual: the flow already sent, available to undo
Augmenting paths are found in the residual graph
Backward edges let the algorithm reroute earlier decisions

blocks.text: The residual graph is the single most important concept here. It reframes remaining capacity and cancellable flow as ordinary edges you can search over.
Because both forward slack and backward undo appear as residual edges, one BFS or DFS can find any way to improve the flow.
A neat implementation detail: storing capacities in a matrix lets a single entry represent both the remaining forward capacity and, in its mirror, the backward capacity.

The Ford-Fulkerson method is the general procedure built on these ideas. It starts with zero flow and repeatedly finds an augmenting path in the residual graph, pushing the bottleneck amount each time.

blocks.caption: Repeatedly find an augmenting path and add its bottleneck until none remain
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406762092-564007238.png

items: Start with flow equal to zero everywhere
Find any augmenting path from source to sink in the residual graph
Push flow equal to the bottleneck along it, updating residuals
Repeat until no augmenting path exists
The accumulated flow is then maximum

blocks.text: When no augmenting path remains, the flow cannot be increased, and it is provably the maximum. That guarantee comes from the max flow min cut theorem, covered in its own topic.
Ford-Fulkerson is a method rather than a single algorithm, because it leaves open exactly how each augmenting path is chosen.
Different choices of path lead to different concrete algorithms, such as Edmonds-Karp and Dinic.
Ford-Fulkerson does not say how to find each augmenting path. Edmonds-Karp pins that down: always find the shortest augmenting path, using a breadth first search.
Choosing the shortest path by number of edges gives a clean polynomial time bound and avoids the pathological slowness that can happen if you pick paths carelessly.

codes.python:
from collections import deque
def maxflow(n, s, t, cap):              # cap is an n x n capacity matrix
    total = 0
    while True:
        parent = [-1] * n
        parent[s] = s
        q = deque([s])
        while q:                         # BFS for a shortest augmenting path
            u = q.popleft()
            for v in range(n):
                if parent[v] == -1 and cap[u][v] > 0:
                    parent[v] = u
                    q.append(v)
        if parent[t] == -1:
            break                        # no augmenting path left
        bottleneck = float("inf")
        v = t
        while v != s:
            bottleneck = min(bottleneck, cap[parent[v]][v])
            v = parent[v]
        v = t
        while v != s:
            cap[parent[v]][v] -= bottleneck   # use forward capacity
            cap[v][parent[v]] += bottleneck   # add backward capacity
            v = parent[v]
        total += bottleneck
    return total

blocks.text: By always taking the shortest augmenting path in edges, Edmonds-Karp guarantees a polynomial number of augmentations regardless of the capacity values.
The code represents the network as a capacity matrix and updates it in place, so the same matrix doubles as the residual graph.
The single most confusing part of network flow is why we allow pushing flow backward. The reason is that early greedy choices can be wrong, and backward edges let the algorithm fix them.

Suppose an early path routes flow through an edge that, in hindsight, blocks a better overall routing. A later augmenting path can send flow along that edge backward residual, effectively cancelling the earlier flow and redirecting it. Without this, the method could get stuck below the true maximum.

Undo built in:

Backward residual edges are a built in undo button. They let a later path reroute earlier flow, which is exactly why augmenting paths reach the true maximum rather than a dead end.
Without backward edges, a greedy first path could permanently waste capacity and trap the algorithm below the true maximum.
With them, no early decision is ever final, because a later path can always reroute flow through the backward residual.
This undo mechanism is the deep reason a purely greedy approach fails but the residual based method succeeds.
The running time depends on how augmenting paths are chosen, which is why the specific variant matters.

items: Generic Ford-Fulkerson: depends on the flow value and may be slow with bad path choices
Edmonds-Karp, using BFS: O(V times E squared), independent of the capacities
Dinic algorithm, an advanced variant: O(V squared times E), much faster in practice
For unit capacity graphs the bounds improve further

blocks.text: For most purposes Edmonds-Karp is a safe, correct choice, and Dinic is the go to when performance really matters.
The important takeaway is that Edmonds-Karp bound does not depend on the capacities, only on the numbers of nodes and edges, which makes it reliable.
When capacities are huge and performance matters, Dinic algorithm is the usual upgrade.
Network flow is a modeling superpower, because many problems that look unrelated reduce to max flow.

items: Maximum bipartite matching, by connecting a source and sink to the two sides
Assigning tasks to workers under capacity limits
Scheduling and resource allocation problems
Finding edge disjoint or vertex disjoint paths

blocks.text: The bipartite matching reduction is the classic example: add a source linked to every left node and a sink linked to every right node, all with capacity one, and the max flow equals the maximum matching.

items: Maximum bipartite matching
Task and resource assignment under limits
Scheduling with capacity constraints
Edge disjoint and vertex disjoint path counting

blocks.text: The bipartite matching reduction is worth memorising: source to left with capacity one, left to right along allowed pairs, right to sink with capacity one, and the max flow is the matching size.

content.title: 11. The Max Flow Min Cut Connection

blocks.text: Network flow has a deep and beautiful partner result: the max flow min cut theorem. It states that the maximum flow from source to sink exactly equals the capacity of the smallest cut separating them.

A cut is a way of splitting the nodes into a source side and a sink side, and its capacity is the total of the edges crossing from the source side to the sink side. This theorem is why Ford-Fulkerson is guaranteed to be optimal, and it is important enough to have its own topic.

items: A cut separates the source from the sink
Its capacity is the total of edges crossing forward
Max flow always equals the minimum cut capacity
This guarantees the augmenting path method is optimal

blocks.text: This theorem is the reason we can trust the algorithm output. When no augmenting path remains, the flow equals a cut capacity, so it cannot possibly be improved.
It also gives a bonus: the saturated cut tells you which edges form the true bottleneck of the network.

content.title: 12. Pitfalls and How to Approach It

blocks.text: Keep these points in mind when applying network flow.

items: Always include backward residual edges, or the algorithm can get stuck early
Choose Edmonds-Karp or Dinic, not naive path picking, for a good time bound
The real skill is modeling: figure out what the source, sink, and capacities represent
Watch for capacities that must be split, like node capacities modeled by splitting a node in two

blocks.text:
The hard part is modeling:

Implementing max flow is routine once learned. The real challenge, and the interview skill, is recognising that a problem is secretly a flow problem and setting up the network.
A frequent modeling need is a capacity on a node rather than an edge. The standard trick is to split the node into an in copy and an out copy joined by an edge of that capacity.
Network flow turns questions about routing and matching into a single powerful framework.

items: A flow network has capacities, a source, and a sink
Flow obeys capacity limits and is conserved at inner nodes
Augmenting paths in the residual graph build up the maximum flow
Backward residual edges let the algorithm undo earlier choices
Max flow equals the minimum cut, guaranteeing optimality

blocks.text: Whenever a problem is about moving as much as possible through a constrained network, or can be reframed that way, network flow is the tool that solves it.
Hold on to the pipes picture: capacities are pipe widths, augmenting paths open new routes, and backward edges let you reroute water you already sent.
